AI/R Tips
💡 /clear conversations regularly
💡 Use AGENT.md to store regular instructions
💡 Ask agent to “talk like a caveman”: succinct and saves tokens
💡 Create skills to avoid common pitfalls
💡 Use tools like air (formatting), pak (installing packages), rig to manage multiple R installations
💡 Kimi K3 recommended as a capable model for reasonable price


💭 Harness provides the tools, model is specific LLM, provider who runs the server


🚨 NEVER MAKE ANOTHER HUMAN READ AI SLOP


AGENTS.md: instructions the AI reads every session
If AI writes your code, comment as a human
Tip: put “talk like a caveman” in your AGENTS.md — saves tokens and gets to the point.
/clear the Posit AI conversation regularly: conversations are additive and it resends everything in the conversation every time you continue a conversation, increasing the number of tokens used
On tokens:

Tools exist like agentsview.io shows how many tokens you use and what it costs.

AGENT.md is a way to avoid repeating yourself across multiple conversations, apply personal preferences across projects, keep them minimalist and not build them up too much.
Create skills to save tokens by avoiding common pitfalls and to steer it in the right direction to something more efficient
Use tools like air for formatting, pak for installing R packages and rig to manage multiple R installation
Kimi K3 strongly recommended as a very capable model for a reasonable price
Terminology:

“Harness” provides the tools (e.g., Posit AI),
“Model” is the specific LLM (e.g. Kimi K3) and
“Provider” is who runs the server that runs the model (e.g. posit.ai)
An agent is a model, inside a harness, running a loop, using tools, to achieve a goal.

Urge the audience: if you use AI for code, at least edit the comments yourself so a human voice stays in the code.

section: Session that’s stayed with me: Teaching at the Frontier
text:
Session that’s stayed with me: Teaching at the Frontier

with Mine Cetinkaya-Rundel, Marc Dotson, Derrick Cogburn, Christian Martinez



Problem 1:
Teaching how to code in the AI era

Solution:
Teach clear AI best-practices, coding workflow, assess judgement and syntax






Problem 2:
Students learn for a semester, but forget after.

Solution:
Encourage students to reflect, promote active learning through encouragement and feedback


Directly impact my developing pedagogical values as a teacher:
Shifting AI as a shortcut to learning support, and fostering creativity.



This session was eye-opening for me as an academic supervisor and emerging tertiary teacher. This year was my first year as the Head tutor of Coding and Data Analysis in Biomedicine and next year I will assume the role of co-coordinator. I wanted to learn how to teach code effectively and utilise the new tools at our disposal.
The problem is teaching in the AI era is difficult, when students are learning to code but can simply go to AI who can do a pretty good job, but students don’t have the skill set to learn when AI is wrong.
The solution from these experienced teachers suggested to: - Integrate AI guide and prompt engineering into classes throughout semester, provide explicit best AI practices - Don’t expect memorisation; expect knowing how to use and verify code, and assessments can both evaluate the judgement and syntax - There is a clear emphasis on teaching students about workflows and version controls, and shift AI from a shortcut to a learning support - Examples of using an AGENTS.md file or other built-in AI agents with integrated pedagogical guardrails
Another problem is that often when we teach code, students are motivated and learn a lot, but then after the class they forget everything.
Christian Martinez had a striking talk about encouraging students to reflect on their work, and create a profile they can refer back to. He called this the “accidental author” model where students were invited to revise or resubmit previous weekly assignments, and create a public-facing quarto book that they can refer back to, or even add to their CV as a tangible output from the class. Because students make their own books, they get creative and go down fun rabbit holes.
This session directly will impact how I approach my role as co-coordinator next year: i want to balance AI use with fostering creativity

Introducing the commons R package:


How can we design AI systems to produce better work?
Help the agent be correct and make it less bad when wrong (sound statistics, reproducible practices, trusted code)
Do this by providing trusted code known to be correct
Make it less bad when it’s wrong (share your environment and prompts so it nudges you to good choices)
Signals in response of high and low trust
As a teacher/supervisor: This will directly help me ensure students are on the right path when learning how to code.
My angle as a teacher: a way to ensure AI-generated content students rely on is accurate and aligned with what we teach.


Introducing the shinyreact R package:


Browse React.dev components, use them in Shiny
1:1 UI ↔︎ server binding with reactive_output()
.tsx JavaScript file
Slides here
React: 100M+ downloads per month vs. Shiny’s 50M in 14 years.
Before:

Server does reactive computation, client handles UI, loosely coupled.
Before shinyreact: server.R handles reactive computation and the ui.R defines the visual structure by using built-in functions (fluidPage(), sidebarLayout()).

With shinyreact: Replace ui.R with a React component that you write yourself, giving complete freedom of design using the vast React ecosystem.

Now each UI component can be directly linked to its server logic — more efficient, more responsive apps.

text:
New developments that I know will change my life






Provide trusted code to help AI systems


Browse React.dev components, use them in Shiny


Including Quarto2, QuartoHub, quarto-revealjs-editable





 
{mirai}: Async, never wait for a result
{mori}: Shared memory: one copy, many readers

 
{ducklake}: Database versioning in R
{dplyneage}: Column-level lineage for {dplyr}


Tune {tidymodels} in Databricks via tune_grid_spark()




Accessibility in quarto: - Responsibilities of Quarto and the user: both have a role - Quarto devs can create accessible tools based on feedback - User: Colour contrast 4:5:1, Set alternative text, Check docs on multiple devices, Hit tab, Zoom in - Charlotte Wickham. New in Quarto HTML: “skip to main content” on Tab for keyboard-only users. - Your responsibilities: shift-left on accessibility; set alt text (fig-alt in chunks, logo-alt in YAML); colour contrast ratio 4.5:1 (agents are good at writing that CSS). - What can’t be automated: hit the Tab key yourself, zoom to 200%, check on mobile, check computational outputs. Slides: - quarto-revealjs-editable: Move and resize slides by hand - Quarto 2: Rewritten in Rust, ~100x faster - Quarto Hub: Collaborative editor (experimental) - Emil Hvitfelt: - Edit slides with a cursor — drag images, resize — and the code updates after the fact. - Slides: emilhvitfeldt.github.io/talk-quarto-editable. - The future of quarto-revealjs is quarto-revealjs-editable - Allows users to modify slides that make sense for a user-interface - Editable pane, adjust size, and code adjusts after the fact - Carlos Scheidegger: - q2 compiled to WebAssembly runs in the browser, fast enough to re-render at every keystroke; - Collaboration via Automerge (CRDT); LLM agents can be collaborators via MCP. Roadmap ~1 year from Quarto 1 → 2; HTML furthest along. - Quarto 2: Rewritten in Rust: 100x faster than Quarto – fast enough to render at a key stroke, and can sync source and visual editors nicely - QuartoHub: Collaborative editor for Quarto documents (experimental): features real-time rendering, browser-based editor, comments, track changes (both who made the change and what the change is) - “Quarto wasn’t built for AI — it’s rooted in plain text and reproducibility… better when your collaborator is also an agent; consider asking for a qmd file.” - A Shiny server is an event loop; long tasks block it for every user. - Scaling safely: queues fill; a dispatcher dying stops everything; no dispatcher strands tasks behind slow ones. mirai: if a daemon dies, only its queue goes with it. - Bounded queue + try_mirai(): set a memory limit; on overflow it returns NULL so you control the fallback (warn, retry). - mori::share(): put one dataset in shared memory once — 100 tasks read one copy, so your app supports many more users. - Scales: desktop → your servers over SSH → HPC (cluster_config()) → Kubernetes/Workbench launcher. Not just Shiny — tidymodels integration is coming. - bronze → silver → gold — each hop a versioned, documented transaction - Travis Gerke, “Quack to the Future”: attach the database; every change is version-controlled. - Medallion: bronze = raw as received; silver = cleaned, conformed types and names; gold = analysis-ready with business logic. - Also dplyneage: column-level lineage for dplyr pipelines — every column traced back to its sources. Slides: tgerke.github.io/quack-to-the-future.

#'
#' @return An S3 object of class `control_grid` (also used for `control_bayes`,
#' `control_resamples`, `control_last_fit`) used to contain the
#' control settings in a grid search as a list.
#'
#' @examples
#'
#' library(recipes)
#' library(rsample)
#' library(parsnip)
#' library(workflows)
#'
#' set.seed(1234)
#'
#' folds <- vfold_cv(mtcars, v = 5)
#'
#' recipe <- recipe(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars) |>
#'   step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
#'
#' # Model with tuning parameters, used for `tune_grid()` and `tune_bayes()`.
#' spec <- mlp(
#'   hidden_units = tune(),
#'   penalty = tune()
#' ) |>
#'   set_engine("nnet") |>
#'   set_mode("regression")
#'
#' wf <- workflow() |>
#'   add_model(spec) |>
#'   add_recipe(recipe)
#'
#' # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#' # control_grid(): Modify tuning process in `tune_grid()`.
#' ctrl <- control_grid(
#'   # save out-of-sample predictions
#'   save_pred = TRUE,
#'   # print progress while tuning
#'   verbose = TRUE
#' )
#'
#' tune_grid(
#'   wf,
#'   resamples = folds,
#'   grid = 5,
#'   control = ctrl
#' )
#'
#' # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#' # control_bayes(): Modify tuning process in `tune_bayes()`.
#' ctrl_bayes <- control_bayes(
#'   save_pred = TRUE,
#'   verbose = TRUE
#' )
#'
#' set.seed(3246)
#' tune_bayes(
#'   wf,
#'   resamples = folds,
#'   initial = 5,
#'   iter = 10,
#'   control = ctrl_bayes
#' )
#'
#' # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#' # `fit_resamples()` and `last_fit()` can't use `tune()` placeholders, so for
#' # `control_resamples()` and `control_last_fit()` we use a model with fixed
#' # parameters.
#' # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#' # control_resamples(): Retain out-of-sample predictions and fitted workflows
#' # in the grid and each fold.
#' spec_fixed <- linear_reg() |>
#'   set_engine("lm")
#'
#' wf_fixed <- workflow() |>
#'   add_model(spec_fixed) |>
#'   add_recipe(recipe)
#'
#' keep_pred <- control_resamples(
#'   save_pred = TRUE,
#'   save_workflow = TRUE
#' )
#'
#' fit_resamples(
#'   wf_fixed,
#'   resamples = folds,
#'   control = keep_pred
#' )
#'
#' # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#' # control_last_fit(): Control last fit process by printing progress.
#' split <- initial_split(mtcars)
#'
#' ctrl_last_fit <- control_last_fit(verbose = TRUE)
#'
#' last_fit(
#'   wf_fixed,
#'   split = split,
#'   control = ctrl_last_fit
#' )

section: I have often been an AI skeptic…
text:
I have often been an AI skeptic…




But one thing that stood out across the conference was how thoughtfully people are engaging with AI, not as a replacement for human expertise, but as a tool that can enhance creativity, productivity, communication, teaching, and scientific discovery.

Some standout AI sessions (and learnings!)






Wes McKinney’s keynote







Demystifying LLM jargon by example









Build your understanding of problem statement







Do not outsource your thinking and creativity

Consumption vs Creation



Consuming
Talks, docs, packages, other people’s code
How I learn

Creating
Contributing, writing, sharing back
How I can give back


I want to strike a balance between the two, and I’m more inspired to contribute more to the open source community!

Stay curious, stay critical – it’s OK to be a skeptic, but engage thoughtfully with AI
Own the problem – the clearer your problem statement, the more useful AI becomes
Keep the human in the loop – human expertise is what makes AI output trustworthy
Give back – share what you learn: blog it, talk about it, contribute to a package
Find your people – communities like R-Ladies+ are where the creating starts 💜

Advice for Opportunity Scholars 2027

Be active in your R communities
Make a website!
Join R/Tidy Dev Days, Data Hangouts, Hackathons
Compile a list of your R skills

Final thoughts

Humans have never been more important in the unstable AI era



“Before trusting the scores, validate the Judge”
